summary: Deprioritize. The paper (Bali, Cakici and Whitelaw) argues that stocks with extreme positive daily returns are overpriced lottery-like assets, so the lowest MAX decile should beat the highest. We tested a long-only, equal-weight version of the lowest MAX decile on a 415-name S&P 500 survivor universe over 2015 to 2025, and it returned a net CAGR of 6.31% against 12.71% for the equal-weight universe, with a Sharpe ratio of 0.35 against 0.65. The edge fails at 10 bps, holds in 0 of 2 sub-periods, and the ranked groups run the wrong way (rho 0.84), so the paper's pattern did not appear in this sample. In the fund simulation, P(NPV > 0) is 2% and the median incremental fee PV is -$5.0M against the equal-weight universe fund. The paper was read reliably, but the negative performance, weak robustness and negative economics together drive the recommendation.

sections.What the paper proposes: The paper sorts NYSE, AMEX and NASDAQ stocks each month into deciles on MAX, the maximum daily return within the formation month, and holds the deciles for the following month. The economic argument is that investors prefer lottery-like payoffs and many are poorly diversified, so they pay more for stocks with extreme positive daily returns, and those stocks earn lower returns afterward. The experiment we selected is Table I, value-weighted decile portfolios over July 1962 to December 2005. The paper reports decile 10 minus decile 1 at -1.03% per month (Newey-West t = -2.83), so the lowest MAX decile is the favored group and the highest is the disfavored group.
sections.What we implemented and changed: We computed MAX as the rolling maximum daily return over one month, with a minimum of 15 trading days in the formation month, sorted into deciles with equal-count breakpoints, held the lowest decile for one month with no skip, and rebalanced monthly. Execution uses the prior month's last close for the signal and the next month's first trading-day close for trades, with a cost of 10 bps. We adapted five items: weighting is equal rather than value, the strategy is long-only with no short leg, the universe is our 415-name S&P 500 survivor universe rather than all CRSP stocks, the sample is 2015 to 2025 rather than 1962 to 2005, and market capitalization is not used. Four fields were assumed because the paper is silent: the breakpoints, no price floor, 252 days of minimum history, and 15 minimum formation days. Six details are left unresolved by the paper and run on engine defaults, including share-code filters, delisting returns and the timing of market capitalization. 19 names were excluded for missing data.
sections.What the backtest found: Over 132 months, the portfolio held between 31 and 42 names. Net of costs it earned a CAGR of 6.31% against 12.71% for the equal-weight universe, and a Sharpe ratio of 0.35 against 0.65. The Newey-West t-statistics for the monthly shortfall are -2.71027 against SPY and -3.02908 against the equal-weight universe. The four-factor alpha t-statistic is -1.60, reported but not a gate. The robustness test fails at 10 bps, and the edge over the equal-weight universe holds in 0 of 2 sub-periods. The ranked-group result runs opposite to the paper: group rho is 0.84, not in the expected direction, so higher MAX deciles earned more here, not less. Turnover is high, with mean monthly turnover of 0.794486.
sections.What the simulation and economics found: We simulated a long-only fund with 1000 bootstrapped paths under an assumed 2/20 fee schedule with a hard hurdle, measured against an equal-weight universe fund charged the same fees. The fee schedule is an assumption, not an observed one. P(NPV > 0) is 2%, and the median incremental fee PV is -$5.0M against the equal-weight universe fund. The expected incremental fee PV is negative, so no break-even AUM exists. Even after removing the historical underperformance against the equal-weight fund, the share of positive-NPV paths is only about half, so the strategy has no demonstrated edge to monetize. The bootstrap resamples historical days and cannot create regimes absent from the sample.
sections.How reliable the interpretation was: Implementation reliability is amber: 4 fields assumed, 5 adapted, evidence valid for 100% of material fields, and 0 critical check disagreements. Extraction ran once, so agreement across runs is trivially 1.0. Against the preliminary reference, agreement is 0.692308, with one critical error on the wording of the signal formula and three minor errors on required inputs, breakpoints and the headline result. The reference is preliminary, so these scores are indicative. Remaining limitations: the survivor universe flatters returns because delisted names are absent, weighting is equal, the strategy is long-only, the whole sample lies after publication, cash earns zero yield, returns use Yahoo adjusted-close conventions, and effort reduction from the engine is not measured.
sections.What to do next: No further work is warranted on this strategy in its current form. The long-only equal-weight test on post-publication data shows no edge over the equal-weight universe, and a lowest-MAX portfolio loses to its own benchmark and to SPY. If someone wants to revisit it, the open questions are untested here: the paper's value-weighted construction, the short leg, and a point-in-time universe that includes delisted stocks. Resolving the six unresolved details with the original CRSP data would also be needed before treating this as a replication. Until then, the capital and research time are better spent on other candidates.
